las1993.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (Section 1, Computer Aided Dispatch Conclusions, para 1007 x)
las1993.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993.quote: on 26 and 27 October 1992 the computer system itself did not fail in a technical sense. Response times did on occasions become unacceptable, but overall the system did what it had been designed to do. However, much of the design had fatal flaws that would, and did, cumulatively lead to all of the symptoms of systems failure;

las1993_golive.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 4021)
las1993_golive.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_golive.quote: When the system was fully implemented at 07:00 hours 26 October 1992 the system was lightly loaded.
supports: full CAD implementation at 07:00 on 26 October 1992

las1993_demand.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (Section 1, para 1007 w)
las1993_demand.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_demand.quote: the 26 and 27 October 1992 were not exceptionally busy days in terms of emergency incidents or patients carried. The increase in calls on those days was largely as a result of unidentified duplicate calls and call backs from the public in response to ambulance delays;

las1993_queue.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 4023)
las1993_queue.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_queue.quote: Starting with effect 4022 d), the number of exception messages increased rapidly to such an extent that staff were unable to clear the queue. As the exception message queue grew the system slowed. The situation was made worse as unrectified exception messages generated more exception messages. With the increasing number of "awaiting attention" and exception messages it became increasingly easy to fail to attend to messages that had scrolled off the top of the screen.
supports: queue depth, not CPU, was the failing quantity

las1993_callbacks.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 4032)
las1993_callbacks.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_callbacks.quote: Turning to telephone communications between the public and CAC, delays to patients and uncovered incidents greatly increased the number of call backs, thus increasing the total number of calls handled. An increased call volume, together with a slow system and too few call takers caused significant delays in telephone answering, thereby further increasing delays to patients.

las1993_ring.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 4004)
las1993_ring.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_ring.quote: Diagram 4.2 shows another indicator of poor service. Average ring times peaked at around 10 minutes on 26 October 1992
supports: average ring times peaked at around 10 minutes

las1993_purge.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 4028)
las1993_purge.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_purge.quote: In summary, effects 4022 b) and c) contributed to incorrect allocations, a slowing of the system and uncovered incidents all leading to delays to patients. The number of uncovered incidents was probably increased when at one stage the exception report queue was cleared in an effort to increase the speed of the system.
supports: draining the queue lost the work in it

las1993_semimanual.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (paras 4033, 4034)
las1993_semimanual.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_semimanual.quote: Following the CAD problems of 26 and 27 October 1992, CAC had reverted to a semi manual method of operation, identical to that which had operated with a variable degree of success before 26 October. [4034] This method of working comprised: a) calls being taken on the CAD system (including use of gazetteer); b) incident details being printed out in CAC; c) optimum vehicle resource identified through contact with nearest station to incident; d) mobilisation of the resource via CAD, direct to the station printer or to the MDT.
supports: incident details printed out in CAC and at station printers

las1993_manual.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 4036)
las1993_manual.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_manual.quote: This system operated with reasonable success from the afternoon of 27 October 1992 up to the early hours of 4 November.
supports: semi-manual working began on the afternoon of 27 October 1992

las1993_price.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (para 3047)
las1993_price.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_price.quote: Once Datatrak had replaced Terrafix in this consortium the Apricot bid at £937,463 was some £700,000 cheaper than the next nearest bid.
supports: £700,000 cheaper than the next nearest bid

las1993_leak.title: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service (paras 4037, 4039)
las1993_leak.author: South West Thames Regional Health Authority
las1993_leak.quote: In carrying out some work on the system some three weeks previously the SO programmer had inadvertently left in the system a piece of program code that caused a small amount of memory within the file server to be used up and not released every time a vehicle mobilisation was generated by the system. Over a three week period these activities had gradually used up all available memory thus causing the system to crash.
supports: para 4037: shortly after 2am on 4 November the system slowed significantly and, shortly after this, locked up altogether

hansard1992.title: London Ambulance Service, HC Deb 28 October 1992 vol 212 cc1013-20
hansard1992.author: Virginia Bottomley, Secretary of State for Health
hansard1992.quote: earlier this afternoon the South West Thames regional health authority accepted the resignation of John Wilby as chief executive of the London ambulance service. Martin Gorham, deputy chief executive of the regional health authority, will take over as acting chief executive of the LAS immediately until a permanent replacement can be recruited.
supports: In Greater Manchester, 97.4 per cent. of responses are made within 14 minutes, but in London the figure is only 64 per cent.
we expect 95 per cent. of calls to receive a response within 14 minutes

unverified: Response times of up to about three hours on 26-27 October 1992. Widely repeated, but the inquiry report gives no such figure in any paragraph opened here; what it does give is Diagram 4.1 (percentage of responses under 15 minutes, below October's average) and average ring times peaking at around 10 minutes.

That John Wilby personally set the 8 January 1992 implementation deadline. Para 6070 says the budget and deadline 'were set by the Chief Executive without discussion with the LAS Board' and does not name him; Hansard names Wilby as chief executive on 28 October 1992.

The claim that the breakdown led to 20 deaths. Para 6091 records that of 26 cases considered by coroners' courts since November 1991, 'not a single one has concluded that the LAS can be blamed for the death of a patient'.
The peak length of the exception-message queue. The report says staff were unable to clear it but gives no count.
Whether the two despatch backlogs on 26-27 October ('awaiting attention' and exception messages) were separate data structures or one list rendered two ways.

Whether the exception report queue was the sole record of an outstanding incident. Para 4028 says only that uncovered incidents 'probably' rose when it was cleared; paras 4018 b) and 4026 describe an 'awaiting attention' list and two-line incident summaries running alongside it, and para 4037 shows voice tapes used to reconcile calls. The claim that the queue was the only such record has been removed from the prose.

What share of the GBP937,463 Apricot bid was software. Para 3046 records the Systems Options quotation for the CAD development as GBP35,000; the GBP937,463 in para 3047 is the whole consortium bid. The prose now calls it the winning bid, not the price of the software.
